[Resource from qmd at qmd://t4-qmd/apps/docs/content/docs/orm/v6/prisma-client/queries/transactions.mdx] 1: --- 2: title: Transactions and batch queries 3: description: This page explains the transactions API of Prisma Client. 4: url: /orm/v6/prisma-client/queries/transactions 5: metaTitle: Transactions and batch queries (Reference) 6: metaDescription: This page explains the transactions API of Prisma Client. 7: --- 8: 9: A database transaction refers to a sequence of read/write operations that are _guaranteed_ to either succeed or fail as a whole. This section describes the ways in which the Prisma Client API supports transactions. 10: 11: ## Transactions overview 12: 13: :::info 14: 15: Before Prisma ORM version 4.4.0, you could not set isolation levels on transactions. The isolation level in your database configuration always applied. 16: 17: ::: 18: 19: Developers take advantage of the safety guarantees provided by the database by wrapping the operations in a transaction. These guarantees are often summarized using the ACID acronym: 20: 21: - **Atomic**: Ensures that either _all_ or _none_ operations of the transactions succeed. The transaction is either _committed_ successfully or _aborted_ and _rolled back_. 22: - **Consistent**: Ensures that the states of the database before and after the transaction are _valid_ (i.e. any existing invariants about the data are maintained). 23: - **Isolated**: Ensures that concurrently running transactions have the same effect as if they were running in serial. 24: - **Durability**: Ensures that after the transaction succeeded, any writes are being stored persistently. 25: 26: While there's a lot of ambiguity and nuance to each of these properties (for example, consistency could actually be considered an _application-level responsibility_ rather than a database property or isolation is typically guaranteed in terms of stronger and weaker _isolation levels_), overall they serve as a good high-level guideline for expectations developers have when thinking about database transactions. 27: 28: > "Transactions are an abstraction layer that allows an application to pretend that certain concurrency problems and certain kinds of hardware and software faults don’t exist. A large class of errors is reduced down to a simple transaction abort, and the application just needs to try again." [Designing Data-Intensive Applications](https://dataintensive.net/), [Martin Kleppmann](https://bsky.app/profile/martin.kleppmann.com) 29: 30: Prisma Client supports six different ways of handling transactions for three different scenarios: 31: 32: | Scenario | Available techniques | 33: | :------------------ | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | 34: | Dependent writes |
  • Nested writes
| 35: | Independent writes |
  • `$transaction([])` API
  • Batch operations
| 36: | Read, modify, write |
  • Idempotent operations
  • Optimistic concurrency control
  • Interactive transactions
| 37: 38: The technique you choose depends on your particular use case. 39: 40: > **Note**: For the purposes of this guide, _writing_ to a database encompasses creating, updating, and deleting data. 41: 42: ## About transactions in Prisma Client 43: 44: Prisma Client provides the following options for using transactions: 45: 46: - [Nested writes](#nested-writes): use the Prisma Client API to process multiple operations on one or more related records inside the same transaction. 47: - [Batch / bulk transactions](#batchbulk-operations): process one or more operations in bulk with `updateMany`, `deleteMany`, and `createMany`. 48: - The `$transaction` API in Prisma Client: 49: - [Sequential operations](#sequential-prisma-client-operations): pass an array of Prisma Client queries to be executed sequentially inside a transaction, using `$transaction(queries: PrismaPromise[]): Promise`. 50: - [Interactive transactions](#interactive-transactions): pass a function that can contain user code including Prisma Client queries, non-Prisma code and other control flow to be executed in a transaction, using `$transaction(fn: (prisma: PrismaClient) => R, options?: object): R` 51: 52: ## Nested writes 53: 54: A [nested write](/orm/v6/prisma-client/queries/relation-queries#nested-writes) lets you perform a single Prisma Client API call with multiple _operations_ that touch multiple [_related_](/orm/v6/prisma-schema/data-model/relations) records. For example, creating a _user_ together with a _post_ or updating an _order_ together with an _invoice_. Prisma Client ensures that all operations succeed or fail as a whole. 55: 56: The following example demonstrates a nested write with `create`: 57: 58: ```ts 59: // Create a new user with two posts in a 60: // single transaction 61: const newUser: User = await prisma.user.create({ 62: data: { 63: email: "alice@prisma.io", 64: posts: { 65: create: [ 66: { title: "Join the Prisma Discord at https://pris.ly/discord" }, 67: { title: "Follow @prisma on Twitter" }, 68: ], 69: }, 70: }, 71: }); 72: ``` 73: 74: The following example demonstrates a nested write with `update`: 75: 76: ```ts 77: // Change the author of a post in a single transaction 78: const updatedPost: Post = await prisma.post.update({ 79: where: { id: 42 }, 80: data: { 81: author: { 82: connect: { email: "alice@prisma.io" }, 83: }, 84: }, 85: }); 86: ``` 87: 88: ## Batch/bulk operations 89: 90: The following bulk operations run as transactions: 91: 92: - `createMany()` 93: - `createManyAndReturn()` 94: - `updateMany()` 95: - `updateManyAndReturn()` 96: - `deleteMany()` 97: 98: > Refer to the section about [bulk operations](#bulk-operations) for more examples. 99: 100: ## The `$transaction` API 101: 102: The `$transaction` API can be used in two ways: 103: 104: - [Sequential operations](#sequential-prisma-client-operations): Pass an array of Prisma Client queries to be executed sequentially inside of a transaction. 105: 106: `$transaction(queries: PrismaPromise[]): Promise` 107: 108: - [Interactive transactions](#interactive-transactions): Pass a function that can contain user code including Prisma Client queries, non-Prisma code and other control flow to be executed in a transaction. 109: 110: `$transaction(fn: (prisma: PrismaClient) => R): R` 111: 112: ### Sequential Prisma Client operations 113: 114: The following query returns all posts that match the provided filter as well as a count of all posts: 115: 116: ```ts 117: const [posts, totalPosts] = await prisma.$transaction([ 118: prisma.post.findMany({ where: { title: { contains: "prisma" } } }), 119: prisma.post.count(), 120: ]);

I have enough. `updateMany()` can only apply **one** set of values to all matched rows (per t4-qmd/apps/docs/content/docs/orm/v6/prisma-client/queries/transactions.mdx, "Batch/bulk operations" section) — it can't give TodoGroup A order=2 and TodoGroup B order=1 in a single call.

For swapping two different values, use `$transaction([...])` with two separate `update()` calls (same file, "Sequential Prisma Client operations" section):

```ts
await prisma.$transaction([
  prisma.todoGroup.update({ where: { id: groupA.id }, data: { order: groupB.order } }),
  prisma.todoGroup.update({ where: { id: groupB.id }, data: { order: groupA.order } }),
]);
```

This runs both updates atomically as one transaction, so the two orders swap consistently. Note: if you're on a newer Prisma 8-style client, `$transaction([...])` is removed in favor of `db.transaction(async (tx) => {...})` (per `t4-qmd/apps/docs/content/docs/orm/fundamentals/writing-data.mdx`, line 309) — check which major version you're on.
